question: Why does a warm day make the carbon-fixing enzyme in most crops more likely to waste energy?
reference_answer: Higher temperature makes oxygen compete with carbon dioxide at RuBisCO, which increases photorespiration.

The tendency for oxygen to compete with carbon dioxide rises with temperature, because warm leaves hold less dissolved carbon dioxide relative to oxygen, and because plants close their stomata on hot days, which causes carbon dioxide inside the leaf to fall and oxygen to build up. In hot weather, photorespiration can cut the efficiency of a C3 plant by a quarter or more. C3 plants therefore do best in cool, moist climates with moderate light, with an optimum temperature of roughly 15 to 25 degrees Celsius, and their photosynthesis levels off at moderate light intensities. C4 photosynthesis is an adaptation that largely avoids photorespiration. About 3 percent of plant species are C4 plants, but they account for around a quarter of the primary production on land because they include highly productive grasses such as maize, sugarcane, sorghum, and many tropical pasture || ey, soybeans, potatoes, and nearly all trees. In a C3 plant, carbon dioxide that enters through the stomata is picked up directly by the enzyme RuBisCO in the mesophyll cells of the leaf. RuBisCO attaches the carbon dioxide to a five-carbon sugar called ribulose bisphosphate, and the resulting six-carbon compound immediately splits into two molecules of the three-carbon acid 3-phosphoglycerate. Because this is the first stable product and has three carbons, the pathway is called C3. All of the reactions of the Calvin cycle occur in the stroma of the chloroplasts in the same cells. C3 plants have a weakness, which is that RuBisCO can also react with oxygen instead of carbon dioxide. When it does, the plant wastes energy and releases carbon dioxide in a process called photorespiration. answer: A warm day lowers the amount of dissolved CO₂ in leaf cells while O₂ builds up (because warm leaves hold relatively less CO₂ and the stomata tend to close to conserve water). This makes O₂ compete more strongly with CO₂ for RuBisCO’s active site. When RuBisCO fixes O₂ instead of CO₂, the plant undergoes photorespiration, which consumes ATP and releases CO₂ without producing sugar—i.e., it wastes energy. [3][5]

The key to C4 photosynthesis is a division of labor between two kinds of cells. The leaves of C4 plants have a special wreath-like arrangement known as Kranz anatomy, in which a ring of bundle sheath cells surrounds each vein, and these are in turn surrounded by mesophyll cells.
